rationale: A wins because it knows when to kill its own shiny premise. A refuses "Notion's CMEK rollout threatens Microsoft and Google in the enterprise" and admits the residency peg is "Honestly weak as a standalone time hook," while B promotes the same unsupported instinct as "Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents." That discipline matters: a founder can act on A without walking into the reporter's first fact-check.
gaps_in_A: "The cloud-only collaboration tool just added offline editing and customer-held keys - a reversal worth examining" assumes Notion was meaningfully cloud-only and that the launch is a reversal; the update does not prove either.
"before a competitor matches the feature set" invents a competitive clock; no competitor capability or timing appears in the update.
"will pay for control, not features" overstates buyer behavior when the update says no pricing change and only claims regulated buyers were blocked.
"Notion adds EU and Australia data residency as compliance teams tighten on where data lives" needs the current regulatory tightening piece; A flags the weak peg, but the headline still carries it.
gaps_in_B: "quietly testing Notion" adds secrecy the update never gives; "piloting" is the supported word.
"historically seen as too lightweight for their compliance bar" and "consumer-rooted software" are reputation claims from outside the brief.
"Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" is the bad swing: no incumbents, displacement, or replacement evidence is supplied.
"Notion lets EU and Australian enterprise customers keep their data at home" oversimplifies data residency; EU and Australia options are not the same as every customer keeping data at home.
